title: Evidence for megaflood slack-water deposits in the Siyom River Valley, eastern Himalaya – CORRIGENDUM
When and how environmental corporate social responsibility shapes pro-environmental behavior: environmental passion and organizational support as key mechanisms
abstract: Drawing on social cognitive and social exchange theories, this study aims to investigate how environmental corporate social responsibility (ECSR) influences employees’ pro-environmental behavior (PEB), through environmental passion. Additionally, how perceived organizational support moderates the relationship between ECSR, and environmental passion is also explored. The authors tested the conceptual model from dual sources (224 employees and their respective supervisors) in two waves by using a self-administered survey in the Pakistani banking context and used smart PLS for data analysis. The findings revealed that employees’ pro-environmental behavior is driven by their perceptions of organizational efforts on ECSR. Employees’ environmental passion mediated the relationship between ESCR and employee’s pro-environmental behavior, and perceived organizational support toward the environment (POS-E) also found to moderate the relationship between ESCR and environmental passion. These findings hold significant implications in the organization and environmental management domains, helping organizations draft useful strategies to counter environmental degradation issues through sustainable work practices. This study integrates social cognitive and social exchange theories to explain the ECSR–PEB link via environmental passion. Furthermore, it introduces POS-E as a novel boundary condition.

title: Wealth-related inequality across the maternal and child continuum of care in low- and middle-income countries: a cross-country panel analysis using the slope index of inequality
Variability in agbelima production and quality of commercial agbelima, and suitability of provitamin A carotenoid cassava for agbelima production
abstract: Purpose Traditional cassava-based staple foods in sub-Saharan Africa vary in quality and have limited nutritional value. Provitamin A carotenoid (pVAC) cassava varieties with yellow-fleshed colour have been developed to address vitamin A deficiency. This study aims to investigate traditional agbelima processing practices and the physico-chemical and microbiological quality of commercial agbelima, and assess the suitability and consumer acceptance of pVAC cassava varieties for agbelima production. Design/methodology/approach A survey documented processing practices, consumption patterns and quality preferences. Thereafter, 20 commercial agbelima mash samples were analyzed for physico-chemical and microbiological characteristics. Finally, one local white-fleshed and five pVAC cassava varieties were processed under standardized conditions, and the resulting agbelima mash and cooked paste were evaluated for physico-chemical and microbial changes and consumer perception. Findings Traditional agbelima production varied mainly in pressing duration and fermentation practices. Commercial agbelima mash exhibited relatively stable pH (5.1–5.9; p = 0.13), lactic acid bacteria (7.5–8.9 log CFU g−1; p = 0.09) and yeast counts (7.1–8.5 log CFU g−1; p = 0.08), despite variation in organic acid composition. All pVAC cassava varieties produced fermented agbelima with microbiological characteristics comparable to those of the local white-fleshed variety. Purchase intention for pVAC agbelima paste was primarily driven by its stretchability (r = 0.98, p = 0.02). Among pVAC varieties, I083724 most closely matched the local variety in sensory profile and purchase intention. Originality/value This study integrates field-based assessments with laboratory analyses to link product quality and consumer perception of pVAC cassava. The findings support improvements in processing standards and promotion of nutrient-enhanced cassava products.

title: Valuation of short-term rentals as income-producing residential assets: a hybrid-hedonic framework
abstract: Purpose This study examines whether financial performance mediates the relationship between conventional hedonic property attributes and short-term rental value, and whether short-term rentals should therefore be underwritten as hybrid income-producing residential assets rather than as ordinary housing alone. Design/methodology/approach AirDNA listing-performance data were matched with Stellar MLS property and transaction records to create a property-level panel for a major destination market in Central Florida. Panel diagnostics were conducted for cross-sectional dependence, stationarity, serial correlation, heteroskedasticity and model selection, with conservative inference based on Driscoll-Kraay standard errors. Findings Durable tangible attributes, including configuration, accessibility and leisure amenities, are associated with both revenue and sale price. Platform-facing and management-related intangible variables strongly influence financial performance, but most lose direct significance once revenue enters the value equation. A 1% increase in revenue is associated with an approximately 0.349% increase in sale price. The results, therefore, indicate partial mediation for tangible attributes and a predominantly income-based transmission channel for most intangibles. Practical implications Institutional property managers, lenders and appraisers should apply dual-lens underwriting that combines residential collateral analysis with stabilized cash-flow analysis. Verified operating history should inform NOI normalization, repayment-capacity testing and destination-level concentration-risk assessment. Originality/value The paper develops a hybrid hedonic-income framework for valuing short-term rentals and positions the asset class as a form of operating real estate exposure embedded in residential property. It contributes by distinguishing durable collateral features from operator-contingent platform signals and by showing that most intangible effects are capitalized indirectly through financial performance rather than directly into transaction price.

title: The strategic integration of the Youth Employment Service into corporate value chains: an ecosystem perspective on Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment compliance
journal: International Journal of Development and Sustainability
abstract: This paper hypothesises that strategically integrating the Youth Employment Service (YES) into corporate value chains may enhance Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) compliance while advancing inclusive economic outcomes. Established in 2018 as part of South Africa’s transformation policy mix, YES was designed to address youth unemployment by incentivising firms to create quality work opportunities. However, its implementation has often remained peripheral to core business functions. Evolving B-BBEE policy expectations now encourage firms to embed developmental initiatives within operational ecosystems rather than treat them as stand-alone compliance activities. Guided by an ecosystem perspective, the paper emphasises the interdependence of firms, regulatory structures, and implementing partners in co-creating value. A literature-based methodology was employed, drawing on academic publications, policy documents, programme reports, and industry sources related to YES, B-BBEE, and youth employability. The literature suggests that embedding YES participants in skills-intensive segments of corporate value chains may support B-BBEE objectives and youth capability development. Ecosystem-aligned implementation may also strengthen collaboration and contribute to longer-term socio-economic outcomes. The paper addresses the gap between policy intention and corporate practice, positioning YES as a value-creation mechanism aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goals (Goal 4,8 & 10) and South Africa’s National Development Plan.

title: The interplay of social capital, digital transformation and sustainability for designing international marketing strategies: a systematic literature review
abstract: Purpose This study systematically reviews the current literature on the role of social capital in adopting digital technologies and achieving sustainability. The current investigation identifies key insights across social capital, digital transformation and sustainability paradigms, and highlights how these findings guide business organisations in designing international marketing strategies. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted using the PRISMA protocol. In total, 92 peer-reviewed articles out of 403 manuscripts, based on Scopus and Web of Science (WoS) database searches from 1980 to 2025, were identified and selected for conducting a thematic analysis and proposing a theoretical framework. Findings The analysis of this SLR revealed three main themes: (1) social capital for digital transformation, (2) social capital for achieving sustainability and (3) social capital for both digital transformation and achieving sustainability. Several sub-themes were also synthesised under each theme. Key findings include how social capital permits sustained customer-oriented culture, inter-organisational trust and artificial intelligence-based social networks – critical aspects for designing international market strategies. A potential theoretical framework is also proposed to explain how social capital influences the adoption of digital technologies and the achievement of sustainability goals, and how firms can entrench these identified attributes into sustained knowledge management, improved strategic positioning and market-oriented innovation. Originality/value This is the first study to propose a theoretical framework that connects social capital to digital transformation and sustainability in the context of international marketing. It offers practical insights for firms seeking to integrate social capital, digital technologies and sustainability initiatives into global strategy development.

title: The correct use of the unit symbols U/L and IU/L
“Uroboros” circle: a multilevel study on leader–follower and follower–leader crossover
abstract: Purpose The literature on the crossover theory (Westman, 2001) typically focuses on how leaders influence followers’ well-being by exchanging psychological states and resources (Hobfoll et al., 2018). However, the role of followers in influencing leaders’ well-being has been less explored. Based on the crossover theory and followership theories (Uhl-Bien et al., 2014), this study aims to investigate the circular process of influence between leaders and followers, examining their mutual ability to exchange resources, even during a crisis. Design/methodology/approach A sample of 607 physicians led by 70 head physicians from Italy participated in a survey during the COVID-19 pandemic. The data were analyzed using multilevel structural equation modeling. Two independent models were tested. Findings Results show that, first, head physicians’ dedication (a component of work engagement) influences followers’ dedication and job satisfaction by articulating a vision, which proved effective during the crisis. Second, followers are also able to influence leaders’ dedication through their own dedication. Originality/value This study contributes to the crossover theory applied to the leader–follower relationship by highlighting that followers can influence leaders, offering insights into crisis leadership. It demonstrates the potential for a resource exchange between physicians, even during a period such as the management of the pandemic. Leaders and followers can benefit from their relationship, while human resources managers should be aware that followers, by playing an active role, can support leaders by influencing their well-being in a reciprocal resource exchange, thereby benefiting from the circular nature of the leader–follower relationship.
